topic.title: Treatment Effects under Confounding and Selection Bias
topic.overview: Treatment-effect estimation asks how outcomes would change under an intervention, including how effects vary between individuals. These papers study observational data, randomized evidence, proxy variables, instruments, and partial identification. The missing counterfactual makes this different from ordinary prediction: an accurate outcome model does not by itself establish a valid causal comparison.
topic.whyItMatters: Decisions about interventions need an account of who receives treatment and why. Explicit assumptions and uncertainty can prevent precise-looking estimates from concealing hidden confounding, selection effects, or differences between study populations.
topic.evolution: The representatives move from therapy-effectiveness and dose-response modeling to heterogeneous effects, proximal methods, and combining environments. Recent work considers budgeted experiments, abstaining from uncertain responder classifications, and diagnosing mechanisms behind observational bias. These are complementary ways to make the limits of available evidence more actionable.
openQuestions: When can additional experiments resolve important ambiguities left by observational data?
How can bias mechanisms be distinguished when multiple sources operate together?
